utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Mladen Naletilic and Vinko Martinovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Because of the technical problems, we lost a whole morning, so this afternoon we'll sit until 5.00. Each sitting will be 75 minutes, during which we'll have 30 minutes' break. Witness, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper the usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, and thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NV
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, first of all, our Madam Registrar is going to show you a piece of paper with your name on it. Please don't read the name, but if that is indeed your name, just say yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. Because of the technical capabilities and to help our interpreters, after I put a question to you, please start answering not too slowly, not too fast, especially not too fast. This will facilitate our work, and what you say is going to be interpreted. But now I would kindly ask Your Honours to go to private session, which means, Witness, for you, when we say "private session," we want to hide your identity. You have protected measures granted by this Court. And I would also kindly ask you to make sure not to reveal your identity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NV
utterances.text: At the beginning of 1992, we Croats, together with Muslims, Bosniaks, we tried to organise a joint defence from the attacks of the Republika Srpska Army and the JNA. Muslims, Bosniaks refused such cooperation, and they did it in several ways, verbally and practically. President Izetbegovic claimed that that was not his war, although the war was waged in his state. Still he claimed that it wasn't his war, which irritated the members of the Croatian people. At that time, we were forced to try and defend ourselves at the level Dubrava plain by ourselves, and we continued offering cooperation to Muslims, Bosniaks. At the time, our neighbours, Muslims, Bosniaks, would fill the trenches that we were digging to help us defend ourselves from the aggressor. We tried to arm both Croats and Muslims, Bosniaks, and they armed themselves independently from us, and in that way they built a further mistrust. At the beginning of 1992, when the Republika Srpska army occupied and launched an attack on the Dubrava plain, our forces still were not trained, were not armed, were not connected in any way in order to be able to defend such a huge area. The biggest resistance was put up in the Domanovici village sector, where several members of the Croatian Defence Council were killed, and at the same time the people were being evacuated. Muslim leaders in Stolac municipality at the time issued statements to the effect that that was not their war and that they would find another political solution. They didn't allow Muslims to be evacuated, and they welcomed the occupier army of the Republika Srpska in the JNA with flowers in their hand. You can read about that in the Montenegrin press in April of 1992. You will read in those articles how the JNA Army was welcomed. That was the army from Montenegro. And you will read how Muslims welcomed them in Stolac. This was followed by the period of occupation of the Dubrava Plain, during which time the aggressor burned houses of the Croats who had fled. During that period, in that area, if I can remember well, only about 50 Croats remained, and over 5.000 had fled. The 50 who had remained are still missing, and according to some information that I have, none -- no member of the Muslim Bosniak people was harmed during that period. Towards the end of April, if I'm not mistaken, when our forces, the forces of the Croatian Defence Council, were capable of engaging in some attack activities, we launched an operation to liberate the Dubrava Plain, together with some 100 or so members of our brigade who were Muslims, who were Bosniaks, who stayed in Medjugorje and who were trained together with us, who were equipped together with us, so several thousand members of the HVO and some hundred or so Muslim Bosniak members of that brigade. We started replenishing the brigade by calling conscripts. At this point in time, I would like to point out that no Muslim Bosniak conscript, at the moment when the Dubrava Plain was liberated, was harmed in any way. What I am saying is that we did not institute any proceedings against anybody, although I think this should have been done, for the reason of collaboration with the enemy. And just in addition, the Muslim leadership in Stolac, throughout the occupation, collaborated with the occupation government, and during that time, they disarmed and handed back in 50 rifles that they had taken from people who had them. In the documentation that -- not that you have but the documentation that you will search, you will also probably find the documentation on the collaboration of the Bosniak Muslim leadership, i.e. you will find the minutes of the meetings with the leadership of Stolac and the government of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, can you please tell us -- we've heard in this courtroom the testimony saying that Stolac was abandoned by Croats and that's why it fell into the hands of the Serbs. So what happened in Stolac? When was it liberated and by whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NV
utterances.text: Counsel, I believe that I have partly answered your question, but I shall repeat. Stolac is in the southeastern part of the Dubrava Plain and when the Croats attempted to defend the Dubrava Plain and Stolac, they didn't succeed and that was for one main reason. They were not equipped, they were not trained. You cannot establish a unit in a short period of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. time. And the second reason was that Muslims Bosniaks did not cooperate, and I've already mentioned that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Okay. Tell me whether Stolac was liberated later on, and if it was, when did that happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NV
utterances.text: I already said that the HVO forces launched an attack across the Neretva River from the direction of Capljina towards Stolac. They crossed the River Neretva together with some hundred or so Muslims Bosniaks, soldiers, who were organised in a separate unit, and who did not think that the Dubrava Plain should not be defended, who remained with us all that time. So all of us together in April, if I'm not mistaken, liberated the Dubrava Plateau, the Dubrava Plain, and during the liberation of the Dubrava Plateau, we also liberated, or maybe somewhat later, this operation was called Cagalj. So when the Dubrava Plateau was liberated, we also liberated the town of Stolac, so by those forces that I've just mentioned, so these are the forces that liberated it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Why did you start your explanation at that -- with that particular time? How did things develop further on? Because what I'm interested in is 1993 and how things unfolded in the summer of 1993. So can we try to somehow see what the situation was at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NV
utterances.text: Well, I picked out that date as a starting point because I thought it was very important to mention the positions, that is who held what views at that time. And it is a fact that the Croat Defence Council [French translation coming through] Stolac and among those several thousand, there was also a company of Muslims Bosniaks. [French translation coming through] We replenished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We have a channel problem. [French translation coming through]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it better now? Is it better now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, sorry, we have some technical problems here. So will you please move on what you were explaining to us when I interrupted you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NV
utterances.text: Well, the fact is therefore that we liberated, or that is the HVO liberated, that area. After that, we replenished the unit with conscripts of Muslim Bosniak ethnicity. The chief reason for it was that we did not want to raise the question of responsibility since we needed to live together in the same area, and although we, the Croats, liberated it, and they stayed side by side with the Army of Republika Srpska, we nevertheless incorporated them in our forces so that we could continue to peaceably defend this same area from that same aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me something about your brigade. How professional was it? Were they volunteers? Were they home guards or professional troops? Can you tell us something about the composition of the Knez Domagoj Brigade in those terms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NV
utterances.text: Mr. Lawyer, at that particular time, the brigade was made of volunteers, the majority of whom were of pretty much your age. As for the command staff, I believe I remember only two men who were professional officers. [redacted], and the other one a Muslim Bosniak, and [redacted].

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Just please, please, don't, don't, because you might disclose your identity. If necessary, we shall go into private session, but we've understood, I believe. We have understood that there were two of you and who you were. Can you just tell us what is a professional or a home guard brigade? Will you explain, because you're a professional soldier and there were not many of them here, so perhaps it will help the Honourable Court and I'm sure that the Honourable Judges will also have questions. How was the defence organised in 1992, that is 1993? What were the principles governing the defence, and especially in your municipality, in the municipality of Capljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NV
utterances.text: The Knez Domagoj Brigade was made of volunteers, home guards, that is men of some age and volunteers, from three municipalities, or perhaps in a way from the fourth one; that is from the municipalities of Capljina, Neum, Stolac and a small part from the municipality of Ravno. So the brigade was on the front line that I've already indicated. It was that we organised the defence in three shifts as a rule, which means that as a rule - but of course it could be different - one-third would be on the front line for ten or 15 days, and two-thirds would be on a leave at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I see. And was that the general rule for the HVO in municipalities or what shall I describe it? Is it how it was organised throughout the municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is in Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NV
utterances.text: Your Honours, by and large, that is how it was done, but not always. One municipality would provide either a battalion or a brigade, depending on the size.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Sorry, we've lost you again. Can you hear us, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NV
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: We lost the end of your answer, so could you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NV
utterances.text: In the majority of cases, municipalities, that is every municipality, provided one brigade, a municipality of, if I may call it that, normal size. The town of Mostar provided two, but I stand to be corrected, and smaller municipalities provided one battalion each. But from the very beginning, in the majority of these municipalities, there were some small units for special purposes. Later on they grew, merged and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Let me now move on and ask you if anything in particular happened in July, that is towards the end of June or in early July, on the front line that you manned, and if that was so, say what. So when you came to the brigade, you mentioned the beginning of the conflict. When was that? Why? And what for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NV
utterances.text: Your Honours, in July, 1993, my brigade manned the above-indicated front line and it was made of Croats and Muslims Bosniaks. The fighting gradually moved from central Bosnia coming closer to my defence line. I knew that on my left flank there had already been some fighting in Bijelo Polje and Mostar, a bloody conflict, truly, in which Muslims, Bosniaks, had attacked the Croats, the HVO. An interesting question is which Muslims Bosniaks. Well, those selfsame that joined -- who joined the -- my brigade. I mean just as I admitted them, so did my neighbour on the front line around Mostar also admitted them into his units. Between these lines of responsibility was the Bregava Brigade, which was made only and exclusively -- that is, it was an exclusively ethnically pure Muslim unit, which was on my left flank. That brigade tried, without my knowledge, without any concerns, or without asking me, moved behind my back into the liberated area. When I learnt about it, I wrote a letter to the commander of the brigade --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Excuse me. I have to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we go into a private session? Because it is obviously impossible to avoid -- the witness kept talking in the first person, and it's absolutely clear, so could we please go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We will go back to the open session, please, and we'll break here and we'll resume at 10 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we only have 40 minutes to go this afternoon, and, Mr. Prosecutor, we are not expecting you to finish your cross-examination this afternoon. You may continue tomorrow morning at 9.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Shall I begin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, my name is Poriouvaev. I'm an attorney, trial attorney, and I will ask you some questions which stem from your examination-in-chief and which may go also to your credibility as a witness in this trial. Is it your testimony, Witness, that at some point in July 1992 you joined the HVO? Could you explain to the Trial Chamber: How did it come about that you became a member of the HVO? Was there any specific order or something else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NV
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I did not hear your entire question. Can you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry. It's not my problem, I suggest. Witness, is it correct that somewhere in July 1992 you joined the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And how did it come about that you joined the HVO and left the HV?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NV
utterances.text: When the situation calmed down in the Republic of Croatia, upon the invitation of the leadership of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I assumed a duty in the HVO and I was assigned to the Knez Domagoj Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think at this point we should go into private session for some moments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: 4.55 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 28th day of August, 2002, at 9.30 a.m.
